text:
On the sixteenth of September, twelve days after Donald Trump demanded a rate cut, the Federal Reserve raised rates instead.

Hours later, he asked for one percent. Or less.

Since then, the ten-year US Treasury yield has hit five point three five percent, the highest since 2002.

Oil is above one hundred dollars. Inflation in the euro area just jumped to three point eight percent.

And yet the S and P five hundred just set a record.

Something has to give. So here are six forces moving markets right now, the numbers behind each, and what they mean if you own a world ETF in euros.

Force one: Trump versus the Fed. In 2022 and 2023, the Fed took its rate from almost zero to five and a half percent.

Then it cut six times, down to three point seven five by December 2025.

In May 2026, Kevin Warsh, the chair Trump picked, took over. His first move was a hike, to four percent.

Why? Inflation. US prices rose more than four percent a year this spring, and three point four percent in August.

But look inside. Core inflation, without food and energy, is two point four percent, the lowest since 2021. Gasoline is up twenty-seven percent.

This is an oil shock, not an overheating economy. And the Fed is fighting it anyway.

Markets now price an eighty-six percent chance of another hike in December.

He has also threatened to cut off trade with countries that run surpluses with the US, if the Fed doesn't cut.

Trump wants one percent. The market expects more than four. That gap is the first force on this list.
